Rep. VanDuyne’s bill sounds compassionate, but let’s unpack the fine print. Mandating insurers cover diagnostics without cost-sharing shifts the financial burden—premiums will spike, and taxpayers foot the bill through subsidized plans. Section 2(b)(1) allows insurers to impose prior authorization hurdles, creating bureaucratic delays that defeat the purpose of early detection.

Meanwhile, Big Pharma’s MRI and ultrasound manufacturers (like GE) profit from mandated scans while hospitals inflate charges. Real reform would streamline approvals, slash imaging monopolies’ pricing, and cut administrative bloat—not layer more unfunded mandates that insurers pass to consumers.

Early detection matters, but D.C. can’t mandate efficiency without dismantling the red tape causing the problem.
